outcomes: Separate CPU wall-clock latency from device timestamp duration
Explain asynchronous queue submission and explicit completion points
Fuse an affine transform and ReLU while preserving a scalar oracle
Query timestamp and shader-f16 support before requesting optional features
Relate wgpu's f16 feature to concrete Vulkan capability extensions
lessons: Performance begins with a well-defined clock
Choose mixed precision by capability and range

gpu-timestamp.name: GPU timestamp
gpu-timestamp.definition: A device-written counter sampled around GPU work and converted using the queue's timestamp period.
gpu-timestamp.explanation: Timestamp queries measure intervals on the device timeline. The reference writes a timestamp at the beginning and end of each compute pass, resolves 64-bit ticks into a query buffer, copies them to a mappable staging buffer, and multiplies tick differences by nanoseconds per tick. This excludes some host work and does not equal end-to-end latency. The feature is optional, so the program reports unavailable rather than inventing a duration.

wall-clock-latency.name: CPU wall-clock latency
wall-clock-latency.definition: Elapsed CPU-observed time across a precisely stated operation boundary.
wall-clock-latency.explanation: The project's CPU wall clock begins before bind-group creation and command encoding and ends after output mapping completes. It therefore includes host encoding, queue submission, scheduling, GPU execution, output copying, polling, and output readback, while initial buffer and query allocation are outside the boundary. Mapping and decoding the timestamp staging buffer happen after this boundary. Small operations are noisy, so the experiment warms up and reports a median and range over repeated runs.

kernel-fusion.name: kernel fusion
kernel-fusion.definition: Combining adjacent operations into one kernel so an intermediate need not travel through global memory.
kernel-fusion.explanation: Separate affine and ReLU kernels read the input, write an intermediate, read that intermediate, and write output: four storage-value accesses per element. The fused kernel reads input and writes output: two. Fusion also removes one dispatch. These are algorithmic access counts, not measured bus transfers. The chapter measures both GPU plans and checks them against the same `affine_relu_scalar` CPU oracle before drawing any performance conclusion.

mixed-precision.name: mixed precision
mixed-precision.definition: Using more than one floating-point format to trade range and accuracy for storage or arithmetic benefits.
mixed-precision.explanation: The optional chapter path reads f32 input, converts arithmetic to f16, then writes f32 output. It checks `SHADER_F16`, requests the feature only when supported, and creates the f16 pipeline only after that gate; otherwise the same operation runs in f32. Half precision has a much smaller finite range and fewer significand bits, so finite f32 input is not automatically safe. A separate range guard selects f16 only for the bounded teaching fixture.

vulkan-extension.name: Vulkan extension
vulkan-extension.definition: A named set of capabilities that augments a Vulkan implementation beyond core requirements.
vulkan-extension.explanation: At the lower API layer, half arithmetic and half storage are distinct capabilities. `VK_KHR_shader_float16_int8` exposes shaderFloat16 arithmetic, while `VK_KHR_16bit_storage` controls where 16-bit values may be stored. Cooperative matrix extensions add subgroup operations with supported shapes and element types. wgpu normally translates these details into portable features such as `SHADER_F16`; querying before use keeps the program correct across adapters and avoids unsupported shader creation.

checks: Separate and fused f32 outputs from affine_relu_with_gpu match affine_relu_scalar for an odd invocation count
The default run uses warmups and reports repeated CPU wall-clock median and range
Device pass timestamps are reported only when TIMESTAMP_QUERY is supported
The f16 shader is created only when SHADER_F16 is supported
Inputs outside the safe teaching range use the f32 fallback
limitations: The timing experiment is a microbenchmark of one elementwise chain, not an application benchmark
Device pass timestamp sums omit time between passes and differ from the CPU wall-clock boundary
The f16 path demonstrates arithmetic conversion but retains f32 storage
Measured results depend on adapter, driver, clocks, background work, build mode, and workload size
